813.title: A heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26)
813.hook: "I will take away the stony heart... and I will give you a heart of flesh"
813.howItsDone: Jews read Ezekiel 36 among the Latter Prophets, and the promise of a new heart and a new spirit is often studied alongside Jeremiah's covenant written on the heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ezekiel's charge against the shepherds who fed themselves, and God's promise to seek the lost and bind up the broken. Your line was seek the lost. Who did you reach out to? Day eight hundred thirteen.

A stone in your pocket stays the same temperature as whatever is around it. Cold on a cold day, warm in the sun. It doesn't bruise. It doesn't bleed. It also doesn't feel anything, and it can't grow. There are seasons when a heart can start to work like that: after a loss, after a betrayal, after one too many disappointments. It's protection. It's also a kind of stone. Ezekiel, speaking to exiles who have lost their land, their Temple and their king, uses exactly that picture, and then he makes a promise about it.
screen: `A STONE DOESN'T BRUISE.` → `IT ALSO DOESN'T FEEL.` → `A PROMISE ABOUT HEARTS.`

segments.voice: Here is the verse, in the King James words: "A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh." The Hebrew word here is lev, heart, and some readers point out that in the Bible the heart thinks and chooses, not only feels. Read that way, a heart of stone is not just a cold heart. It's a mind that can't take anything new in, a will that won't move. And a heart of flesh is not a weak heart. It's a living one: it can be pressed, it can respond, it can be written on. That connects back to Jeremiah, a week ago, and the covenant, a line no exile can carry off. You can't write on stone without a chisel. You can write on flesh with a touch. Notice who does the work in the verse. Ezekiel doesn't say, soften your hearts. Earlier in the book, he does tell the people to make themselves a new heart. Here, it's the other way: I will give you, I will take away, I will put within you. Both lines sit in the same book, and some readers hold them together: a person turns, and is also helped to turn. The verse right after says the new spirit will help the people walk in God's ways. And it's spoken to a whole people, not one person. In Hebrew the you is plural. It's a promise to a community gone hard: you will be able to feel again. Flesh is more vulnerable than stone. That's the gift.
screen: `A NEW HEART, A NEW SPIRIT.` · `LEV: THE HEART.` · then, large: `I WILL GIVE YOU AN HEART OF FLESH.` · then: `MAKE YOURSELVES A NEW HEART.` · `FLESH IS MORE VULNERABLE. THAT'S THE GIFT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: soften one hard place in you. Settle, and breathe. Put a hand on your chest if you like. Ask, gently: where have I gone a little bit stone? Maybe toward one person. Maybe toward a place, or a part of your past, or a kind of news you've stopped letting in. Don't force it open. Just notice it, and breathe toward it, the way you'd warm cold hands. Flesh, not stone. If you pray, you can say the verse as a prayer: a new heart also will I give you. The bell holds the time.
A heart of flesh. Ezekiel's promise that God will take away the stony heart and give a living one that can feel and change. Today's word.
Your line: a heart of flesh. Today, toward the one place you found, let in one thing you'd usually keep out: a call, a story, an apology. Day eight hundred thirteen.

814.title: Can these bones live? (Ezekiel 37:1–14)
814.hook: the valley of dry bones, read on the Shabbat of Passover
814.howItsDone: Jews read Ezekiel 37:1–14 as the prophetic reading on the Shabbat during Passover, and Jewish prayer speaks of God who gives life to the dead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a promise to take away the stony heart and give a heart of flesh. Your line was a heart of flesh. What did you let in? Today, Ezekiel is set down among things far harder than stone. Day eight hundred fourteen.

The hand of the Lord takes hold of Ezekiel and sets him down in the middle of a valley, and the valley is full of bones. He's led around them, round about, the text says, and he sees there are very many, and they are very dry. Not a battlefield from last week. Bones bleached and scattered, long past anyone's grief. And then comes the question, put to the prophet as he stands there: "Son of man, can these bones live?"
screen: `SET DOWN IN A VALLEY.` → `VERY MANY, VERY DRY.` → `CAN THESE BONES LIVE?`

segments.voice: Ezekiel's answer is short and honest. In the King James: "O Lord GOD, thou knowest." He doesn't say yes. He doesn't say no. He hands the question back. Then he's told to speak to the bones: "O ye dry bones, hear the word of the LORD." And as he speaks, there is a noise, a shaking, and the bones come together, bone to its bone. Sinews come, then flesh, then skin covers them. And the text stops on a chilling detail: there was no breath in them. Bodies, and nothing more. So he's told to speak a second time, to the wind, the breath. The chapter keeps returning to one Hebrew word, ruach, and the King James renders it breath, wind and spirit. Come from the four winds, O breath. The breath comes into them, and they live, and stand up on their feet, a great army. Then the chapter tells us what the vision means, so we don't have to guess. These bones are the whole house of Israel, and they're saying: "Our bones are dried, and our hope is lost." A people in exile, saying we're finished. And the answer: I will open your graves, and bring you into the land of Israel, and put my spirit in you, and you shall live. Some readers hear in it the return of an exiled people to their land. Others hear it as a promise of the resurrection of the dead, a belief Jewish prayer holds. The rabbis of the Talmud even argued about whether it really happened or was a parable. And Jews read this chapter in synagogue on the Shabbat that falls during Passover, the festival of a people brought out alive.
screen: `O LORD GOD, THOU KNOWEST.` · `BONE TO ITS BONE, BUT NO BREATH.` · then, large: `COME FROM THE FOUR WINDS, O BREATH.` · then: `OUR HOPE IS LOST, AND THE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: revive something you thought was dead. Sit still first, like the bones before the breath came. Then notice the breath arriving on its own, in and out, without your help: ruach, the word the chapter keeps using. Let four breaths come that way. Now bring to mind one thing you've written off: a skill your hands used to know, a song you stopped singing, a room in the house you've stopped using. Ask the question honestly: can this live? You don't have to answer. You can say what Ezekiel said: thou knowest. If you pray, you can offer it to God. The bell holds the time.
Ruach. Hebrew for breath, wind, spirit: the question put to Ezekiel in a valley of dry bones, before it comes into them and they stand. Today's word.
Your line: bone to its bone. Today, take one small step toward the thing you found: one sentence, one call, one minute of practice. Day eight hundred fourteen.

815.title: Two sticks (Ezekiel 37:15–28)
815.hook: the sticks of Judah and Joseph become one in the prophet's hand
815.howItsDone: Jews read Ezekiel 37:15–28 as the prophetic reading for the Torah portion Vayigash, where Joseph and Judah meet, and the hope of gathering the scattered appears in daily prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a valley of dry bones, and a question: can these bones live? Breath came from the four winds, and they stood. Your line was bone to its bone. What small step did you take? Today, the same chapter goes on, with two pieces of wood. Day eight hundred fifteen.

Two sticks. That's all Ezekiel needs for today's message. No vision this time, no fire, no wheels. Just two ordinary pieces of wood. He's told to write a name on each one. On the first: For Judah, and for the children of Israel his companions. On the second: For Joseph, the stick of Ephraim, and for all the house of Israel his companions. Two names that stood for the two kingdoms, south and north, and the north had been carried off and scattered. And then he's told to hold them.
screen: `TWO PIECES OF WOOD.` → `ONE FOR JUDAH, ONE FOR JOSEPH.` → `HOLD THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the instruction, in the King James words: "And join them one to another into one stick; and they shall become one in thine hand." From where the people stand, it looks like this: two sticks, end to end, held in one fist. The prophet's hand closes around the seam. It's street theater, and it's meant to make people ask. So the text gives them their question: wilt thou not shew us what thou meanest by these? And the answer comes: God will take the stick of Joseph and join it with the stick of Judah, and make them one stick, and they shall be one in mine hand. Notice the shift. First, one in thy hand, the prophet's. Then, one in mine hand, God's. In the text, the prophet's small act pictures something God says he will finish. Then the promise is spelled out. The scattered will be gathered from among the nations and brought home. And this line: they shall be no more two nations, neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any more at all. One king. One people. A covenant of peace. And God's dwelling place with them. Remember the north falling, a few weeks back, its people carried off to Assyria. This is where a prophet says the story isn't over. Jewish tradition carries the hope of gathering the scattered in its prayers. But the image also works at kitchen-table size. Two people who stopped speaking. Two halves of a family. Two parts of yourself that don't get along. The prophet doesn't glue the sticks. He holds them together in his hand, and waits for the rest.
screen: `WRITE A NAME ON EACH STICK.` · then, large: `THEY SHALL BECOME ONE IN THINE HAND.` · then: `THY HAND, THEN MINE HAND.` · `NO MORE TWO KINGDOMS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: join two divided things. If there's a pen, a spoon or a twig nearby, pick up two of them. If not, just open your hands. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind two things that are split apart: two people, two sides of a family, two parts of your own life. Let one rest in each hand. Then, slowly, bring your hands together and hold them as one. Don't solve anything. Just feel what it's like to hold both. If you pray, you can place them in God's hand. The bell holds the time.
Two sticks. Ezekiel writes Judah on one and Joseph on the other, and holds them so they become one in his hand: a promise that the divided will be joined. Today's word.
Your line: one in thy hand. Today, do one small thing that brings two divided people, or two parts of your life, a little closer together. Day eight hundred fifteen.

816.title: The river from the Temple (Ezekiel 47:1–12)
816.hook: a river deepens and heals the salt sea; everything lives where it goes
816.howItsDone: Jews read Ezekiel 47 within the book's closing vision of a rebuilt Temple (chapters 40–48), and the Talmud remembers Hananiah ben Hezekiah working through those chapters to reconcile their laws with the Torah's.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two sticks, Judah and Joseph, joined into one in the prophet's hand. Your line was one in thy hand. What did you bring a little closer together? Today, the last of our days in Ezekiel. Day eight hundred sixteen.

Ankles. Knees. Waist. Then water to swim in. That's the order Ezekiel walks into the water. Near the end of his book, he's shown a vision of the Temple rebuilt, and his guide brings him back to the door of the house. There's water seeping out from under the threshold, flowing east. A trickle. The guide walks out with a measuring line, measures a distance, and leads Ezekiel through: the water is to his ankles. Another measure: to his knees. Another: to his loins. Another, and it's a river he can't cross, waters to swim in.
screen: `WATER UNDER THE THRESHOLD.` → `ANKLES, KNEES, WAIST.` → `A RIVER TOO DEEP TO CROSS.`

segments.voice: Water that seeps out under a door usually spreads out and soaks away. This water does the opposite. With no stream feeding it that the text mentions, it keeps getting deeper. Then the guide asks Ezekiel a question: son of man, hast thou seen this? And he's brought back along the bank, and now he sees trees, very many trees, on both sides. The river flows down into the desert and into the sea, and the waters are healed. Here's the line the whole chapter turns on, in the King James words: "every thing shall live whither the river cometh." Fishermen will stand on the shore and spread their nets, and the fish will be many. The trees along the banks will bear fruit every month, and their leaves won't wither. And the last detail: "the fruit thereof shall be for meat, and the leaf thereof for medicine." Food and healing, from water that started under a door. Ezekiel's book began with exiles sitting by a foreign river, the Chebar, far from the Temple. Near its end, a river flows out from the Temple, so deep it can't be crossed, bringing life even to the sea. Some readers hear it as God's presence flowing out from the house. And notice where it starts: not as a river at all, but as a seep under a door, measured again and again as it goes.
screen: `A SEEP UNDER THE DOOR.` · `IT KEEPS GETTING DEEPER.` · then, large: `EVERY THING SHALL LIVE WHITHER THE RIVER COMETH.` · then: `FRUIT FOR MEAT, LEAF FOR MEDICINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one thing grow deeper. Settle, and breathe. Find something in your life that's still at the ankles: a practice you just started, a friendship that's new, something you're learning. Maybe even this daily habit. Don't push it. Just picture walking a little farther into it. Ankles, then knees. What would the next step deeper look like? Five more minutes. One more question. Showing up again tomorrow. Let the breath be the measuring line, one length at a time. If you pray, you can ask that it bring life where it goes. The bell holds the time.
The river from the Temple. Water from under the Temple door grows deeper as it flows, until it heals the sea and everything lives where it goes. Today's word.
screen: `THE RIVER FROM THE TEMPLE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: everything lives where it flows. Today, take the next step deeper into the one thing you found, even if it's only ankle-deep for now. Day eight hundred sixteen.

817.title: Twelve small books
817.hook: twelve short prophets, written together on one scroll
817.howItsDone: In Jewish Bibles the twelve short prophets, Hosea through Malachi, are grouped as one book called Trei Asar, and passages from them are read as haftarot in synagogue.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a river ran out from under the Temple door in Ezekiel's vision, rising as it went, until the salt sea was healed. Your line was everything lives where it flows. What did you let grow a little deeper? Today, Ezekiel's book closes, and a crowded scroll opens. Day eight hundred seventeen.

How do you keep a small book from getting lost? Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel each fill a long book of their own. After them come twelve more prophets, and some of their books are short enough to read on a bus ride. A herdsman from Tekoa. A man who ran from God by ship. A prophet who spoke against one neighboring nation, Edom. Instead of twelve little scrolls, tradition wrote them end to end, on one. Today's word is that scroll's name.
screen: `ONE SCROLL, TWELVE NAMES.` → `SHORT ENOUGH FOR A BUS RIDE.` → `WRITTEN END TO END.`

segments.voice: Trei Asar. It's Aramaic, and it simply means twelve. Not the twelve prophets, not the minor ones. Just: the Twelve. Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi. Say the names out loud once and they start to sound like a class roll call. Now, why one scroll? The Talmud, in tractate Bava Batra, asks a question about the order of the prophets. Near the start of Hosea's book come the words, the beginning of the word of the LORD by Hosea, and the rabbis take that to mean his prophecy came early. So why isn't his book placed before Isaiah? Their answer is plain. Hosea is written together with the last prophets, Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi. And because his book is small, it might get lost. A short scroll can slip behind a shelf. Twelve short books, sewn into one, stay found. So the scroll is a kind of protection for the quiet ones. And quiet is only on the outside. Inside these pages: a prophet whose broken marriage becomes a picture of God and Israel. A prophet who asks for justice to well up as waters. A runaway swallowed by a great fish. Lines still read aloud in synagogue. In the Talmud's list of the prophets, the Twelve appear under that one name, as a single book. Which is a fair picture of how a small voice can last: not alone, but bound in with others. Small books, big voices. Over the next stretch of days, this path walks through the scroll, one prophet at a time.
screen: `TREI ASAR: ARAMAIC FOR TWELVE.` · `HOSEA, JOEL, AMOS… MALACHI.` · then, large: `BECAUSE IT IS SMALL, IT MIGHT GET LOST.` · then: `BOUND IN WITH OTHERS, THEY LAST.`

segments.voice: The practice today is to read one short chapter. If there's a Bible or a reading app nearby, open to any of the Twelve, pick one short chapter, and read it slowly, start to finish, in the time the bell holds. No study notes. Just the words. If you'd rather not read right now, sit with the twelve names instead. Say them once, slowly, and let one of them stay. If you pray, you can ask to hear one small voice clearly today. The bell holds the time.
Trei Asar. Aramaic for twelve: the twelve short prophets, written together on one scroll so none of them would be lost. Today's word.
Your line: small books, big voices. Today, listen for one quiet person in a loud room, and give their words a second hearing. Day eight hundred seventeen.

818.title: Hosea: betrothed again (Hosea 2:16–22)
818.hook: a broken marriage restored becomes a picture of God and Israel
818.howItsDone: Jews who wear tefillin often recite Hosea 2:21–22 on weekday mornings while winding the tefillin strap around the middle finger, and the verses are part of the haftarah for the Torah portion Bamidbar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Trei Asar: twelve short prophets bound on one scroll so none of them would get lost. Your line was small books, big voices. Whose quiet words did you hear twice? Today, the first voice on that scroll. Day eight hundred eighteen.

The first thing Hosea is asked to do is marry. He marries Gomer, and the marriage goes wrong. In the chapters that follow, the book speaks of a wife who goes after other lovers, and it doesn't look away from the hurt. There are children with names that sound like verdicts. There's anger, and accusation, and a house gone cold. A story could end there. This one doesn't. Somewhere in the middle of the second chapter, the voice changes, and a door opens in the wall.
screen: `A PROPHET IS TOLD TO MARRY.` → `THE MARRIAGE BREAKS.` → `THEN THE VOICE CHANGES.`

segments.voice: Hosea's marriage becomes a picture of God and Israel: a covenant like a wedding, a people who wandered after other gods, a love that's been wounded. And in chapter two, God speaks like a husband who wants to begin again. In the 1917 Jewish translation: "I will allure her, And bring her into the wilderness, And speak tenderly unto her." The wilderness. Not as punishment, but as the place where the first love began, after Egypt, before all the trouble. Go back to where it started, and speak gently there. The valley of Achor, a valley remembered for an old trouble, becomes, the text says, "a door of hope." Then a small, sharp change of names. The text says that on that day you will call me Ishi, my husband, and no more Baali. Baali can also mean my husband, but it echoes the name of the god Baal, and the next verse says the names of the Baalim will be taken out of her mouth. The relationship is to be personal again, not one more lord among lords. And then the vows. In the 1917 Jewish translation: "And I will betroth thee unto Me for ever; Yea, I will betroth thee unto Me in righteousness, and in justice, And in lovingkindness, and in compassion. And I will betroth thee unto Me in faithfulness." Betroth, three times. Not remarried, betrothed: back to the very beginning, as if engaged for the first time. And the gifts listed aren't jewelry. They're righteousness, justice, lovingkindness, compassion, faithfulness. Some Jews say these lines each weekday morning, while winding the strap of the tefillin around the finger, like a ring.
screen: `A MARRIAGE AS A PICTURE OF COVENANT.` · `BACK TO THE WILDERNESS, SPOKEN TO GENTLY.` · then, large: `I WILL BETROTH THEE UNTO ME FOR EVER.` · then: `SAID WHILE WINDING THE TEFILLIN STRAP.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to renew one relationship. Sit, and let your breathing slow. Bring to mind one person you've drifted from, or grown used to. A partner, a parent, a friend, a sibling. Go back, in your mind, to the wilderness: to the beginning, when it was new. What did you first notice about them? What did you like? Hold that for a while. Then ask what one word from Hosea's list this relationship needs: justice, kindness, compassion or faithfulness. If you pray, you can say the betrothal line slowly. The bell holds the time.
Hosea. The prophet whose broken marriage becomes a picture of God and Israel, and who hears God promise to betroth the people again. Today's word.
Your line: betrothed again. Today, send the person you thought of one sentence from the beginning: a memory, a thank you, a thing you first loved about them. Day eight hundred eighteen.

819.title: Hosea: take with you words (Hosea 14:2–3)
819.hook: "Take with you words, and return unto the LORD"
819.howItsDone: Jews read Hosea 14 as the haftarah on Shabbat Shuvah, the Sabbath between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and teshuvah, returning, is the theme of that season.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hosea heard God promise to betroth the people again, in righteousness, justice, lovingkindness and compassion. Your line was betrothed again. Did you send that sentence from the beginning? Today, the last chapter of Hosea, and what to bring when you come back. Day eight hundred nineteen.

"Take with you words, And return unto the LORD." That's the instruction, in the 1917 Jewish translation. Not take with you a lamb. Not take with you gold, or a long list of promises. Words. The book of Hosea has spent its chapters on betrayal and hurt, on a people who kept turning away. And at the very end, when the way home finally opens, the one thing they're told to carry is the thing that costs nothing and can be the hardest to find: the right words.
screen: `TAKE WITH YOU WORDS.` → `NOT A LAMB, NOT GOLD.` → `THE HARDEST THING TO FIND.`

segments.voice: The passage opens with one word in Hebrew: shuvah. Return. "Return, O Israel, unto the LORD thy God." Jewish tradition hears in it teshuvah, the word for repentance, which means turning back, coming home. And Hosea doesn't leave the words up to them. He gives them a script. Say unto Him, forgive all iniquity, accept that which is good. Then a strange and striking line. In the King James words: "so will we render the calves of our lips." The 1917 Jewish translation spells out the picture: "So will we render for bullocks the offering of our lips." Bulls were once brought as offerings; here the lips take their place, and words become the offering. Some readers hear in it a quiet idea that the rabbis made central after the Temple was gone: when there is no altar, prayer stands where the sacrifice stood. Sorry, said out loud, becomes a kind of gift. And notice what's asked. Not a feeling first. Words first. Turning back often begins with a sentence that's hard to say, and the saying of it changes something. Hosea knew how hard. That's why he hands them the words. This chapter gives its name to a Shabbat: Shabbat Shuvah, the Sabbath of Return, which falls between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. On it, Jews read this very passage in synagogue, at the season of turning back.

segments.voice: Today's practice: say sorry in plain words. Breathe, and let the week go quiet. Bring to mind one sorry you owe. It may be big, it may be small: a sharp tone, a missed call, a promise that slid. Now do what Hosea does, and write the script. Find the plainest words you can. Not the explanation, not the defense. Something like: I was wrong about this, and I'm sorry. Say it silently a few times, until it sounds like you. If you pray, you can bring the same plain words to God. The bell holds the time.
Hosea. The prophet who ends his book with a way home, and tells the people to take words with them when they return. Today's word.

Your line: take with you words. This week ran from a heart of flesh, through dry bones and a healing river, to Hosea's way home. Today, say the sorry you scripted, in the plain words you found. Day eight hundred nineteen.
